articles.title: THE LORD’S PLACE AND THE BELIEVER’S PLACE
scriptures: Philippians 2:5-8; Luke 23:33,34 (to “they do”); Ephesians 1:19-22 (to “his feet”); John 14:1-3;
articles.meeting: Preaching of the word of God

paragraphs.text: How great is the place that God intends for believers: the greatness of the place of saints who compose the Lord’s precious assembly, their place in glory with Him, and the greatness of the place that is proper to sons. All of that is in God’s mind as the gospel goes out. God is not limited in any of His thoughts; He has full thoughts in mind. There is blessing along the way for men, but what God has in mind is that there might be a great answer secured for Himself, and that involves having believers in the greatest place that we could have.

This scripture in Philippians refers to the Lord Jesus “taking his place in the likeness of men”. That would suggest something distinctive about the place that He took. It was a place that was in divine counsels; it was foretold, it was foreknown. It is said of the Lord Jesus, “thou hast prepared me a body”, Heb.10:5. Then it says, “Lo, I come (in the roll of the book it is written of me) to do, O God, thy will” (v.7). These passages suggest that He came to fill out a place that only He could fill out. It was a place in which He would accomplish the will of God. He took that body which was prepared for Him. Think of the greatness of what had transpired: that the One “who is over all, God blessed for ever” (Rom.9:5) and who as to His Person is from eternity to eternity, took His place in the likeness of men.

A hymn speaks of the incarnation as the wonder of the universe (Hymn 400). You and I were born as we are, and we grow up, we take our part in the human race. But this blessed One, the Lord Jesus – and Scripture guards His Person so carefully – took His place in the likeness of men. You can never limit Him, but He was and is a real man. He took His place as a man; He came into the place of obedience. You think of that: the gospel tells us of the movements of that One, who was God and who descended. Ephesians speaks of Him as “he that descended” (chap.4:10). It is almost used as a title: “He that descended is the same who has also ascended up above all the heavens”. It is the same One; He who descended is the same One who ascended up. In those blessed movements, One who was God descended to take His place here among men, and now as man He has gone up beyond the heavens.

What glory there is in those blessed movements. Philippians brings out that He emptied Himself and took a bondman’s form. What condescending grace, that He should take such a form. It says in Matthew, “the Son of man did not come to be served” (chap.20:28). Think of all that belonged to Him as God, yet He said, ‘I have not come to be served but to serve’. What grace was seen in the One who came to serve His God and Father. Taking that place involved Him doing everything, and completing everything, and glorifying God in doing so. It was a place of perfect obedience – as the scripture brings out, obedience even as far as death. He took that place so that the heart of the blessed God should be told out. What a place He came into, in order that you and I could know the favour and grace and love of the Saviour God.

Titus says, “For the grace of God which carries with it salvation for all men has appeared” (chap.2:11). How has that grace been made known to us? It has been made known as Jesus came in and took His place amongst men. Think what came under God’s eye in that: you cannot but rejoice at it. We look within ourselves, and we see failure and weakness and corruption and the operation of sinful flesh. And what is the answer to it? The answer begins with One who came under the eye of God as taking His place in the likeness of man. He came in in obscurity; yet it was God moving into the sphere that He had created. There were those, the shepherds and the magi, who were led by God and recognised the significance of the Lord’s birth, but otherwise He was in obscurity. It was not unknown in heaven! The heavens were moved when Christ came in, and there was joy in heaven. The whole heavenly sphere was moved when that One took His place in obscurity and smallness and dependence. That was His place, and it was a place of obedience even as far as death: a Man found here in absolute perfection under the eye of God. How distinctive that place was, and how wonderfully it was filled out by the One who took “a bondman’s form”, and who took “his place in the likeness of men”.

In Luke’s gospel it speaks of “the place”: “And when they came to the place which is called Skull, there they crucified him”. It is very stark: “the place”. I believe that God has marked that place where the Saviour was crucified. It speaks in Revelation as to the witnesses whom John saw were killed after their public service, “and their body shall be on the street of the great city, which is called spiritually Sodom and Egypt, where also their Lord was crucified” (chap.11:8). God has marked that place. Things pass under the eye of God and they are marked. God had marked the place of the Lord Jesus in Jerusalem. In the street of that city, He had lifted up His voice with an appeal: “If anyone thirst, let him come to me and drink”, John 7:37. He appealed to men there, and we know that He approached and wept over the city (Luke 19:41). Think of the Lord’s feelings in the face of the rejection of His people. He had come to Jerusalem and had ridden in on an ass: “all this came to pass, that that might be fulfilled which was spoken through the prophet, saying, Say to the daughter of Zion, Behold thy King cometh to thee, meek, and mounted upon an ass, and upon a colt the foal of an ass”, Matt:21:4,5. How that blessed One made Himself available.

It says, “when they came to the place which is called Skull, there they crucified him”. I would say, that was not His place. The will of God involved that He should go that way, but that place was not proper to Him: it was not His place; but it was my place. Any one with sensibility about their sins and their sinful condition, who is aware of what they have done in their sinful history, knows that that was their place. The Lord went there vicariously for us: He hung there amidst all the mocking and the shame and the scorning; He took “the place”. The crucifixion, where they crucified Him, brings home to us what is really in man’s heart, and in mine. It was all told out there. We learn everything at the cross. If we would learn what is in our hearts, we come to the cross and see the Lord Jesus there as the object of man’s hatred. That is what the flesh is in me; it hates Christ. Let us see it for what it is. He came into that place of greatest reproach and then the place of judgement; that was my place. We see what God is in respect of sin, how He assesses it; we learn it there. If we want to know what sin means to God, we look at the One who bore the judgement, the judgement of God. He went down bearing the sins of all those that trust Him, and He bore before the eye of a righteous God all that sin is in its awfulness to God. Christ bore the wrath, bore the judgment – that happened in the place where everything was worked out before the eye of a righteous God. It was the place of judgment. Every one who has put their faith in that work has the assurance that everything was completed there, in “the place”. “There they crucified him” at “the place which is called Skull”.

What was done drew out the intercession of the blessed Saviour Himself. “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do”. The Lord was asking the Father that everything that was done to Him by men at the cross should be counted as the sin of ignorance: He said, “they know not what they do”. That spirit was seen after the Holy Spirit came down at Pentecost; Peter says, “I know that ye did it in ignorance”, Acts 3:17. How great the grace of God, for He had seen His Christ hung publicly between two common criminals. When Peter says, “I know that ye did it in ignorance”, he was speaking in the spirit of the Lord’s own words. Paul says, “for had they known, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory”, 1 Cor.2:8. The cross was a public matter; publicly the last the world saw of the Lord Jesus was on the cross, hanging between two common criminals. God is going to put that matter right. He has marked the place. All passes under His eye, and He will put that matter right, and the assurance of that is the place that God has given Him and which He has now filled.

That led me to Ephesians. What an answer there is to Christ’s suffering and death: God has raised Him from amongst the dead in the might of His strength. Think of the great reserves of divine power that were called forth in raising that blessed One. God, you might say, reserved His power for that One, and He has raised Him from among the dead. Then it says, “and he set him down at his right hand in the heavenlies, above every principality, and authority, and power, and dominion, and every name named, not only in this age, but also in that to come”. That is where Christ is now; and believers in Him, those who have faith, are in the secret of it. We do not see all things subjected to Him yet (Heb.2:8): that awaits God’s timing, and we can be assured as to that, that God is going to vindicate that Man: that is a matter of utmost importance to God, that Christ will be vindicated in the face of all that man meted out to Him. You wonder at the grace of God: He is going on with men, and is going on in the glad tidings. How great is the patience and the long suffering of God. He is saying, as it were, ‘I am holding off the time of judgment in order to save you, to save souls’. The vindication of Christ is a matter of utmost importance in the mind of God, and that time is being held over, up to this moment, for the gathering in of souls.

How great the grace of God, and the day of grace; we speak of it being extended. We mean by that, that God is going on with men. But there is a day in which Christ will be vindicated publicly, and the believer rejoices in that prospect. If we have been brought to appreciate Him, and have come to love Him for what He is, and to know Him as the One who took upon Himself vicariously all that was justly due to us, we rejoice in the fact that He will be publicly vindicated – when it will be demonstrated and recognised that He has rightly been given a place of supremacy, for God has “set him down at his right hand in the heavenlies, above every principality, and authority, and power, and dominion, and every name named”. For the believer, that is the reality now; it awaits the coming day for it to be made publicly manifest. And although we as believers see not all things yet subjected to Him, yet by faith we see Jesus “crowned with glory and honour”, Heb.2:9. That is the place that is now His, and He is wholly worthy of it; it is His by right.

That is something that we come to as we grow in our appreciation of Him, and we can say with full assurance that what God has done with Jesus is right. God will always do what is right. Abraham could say that: “Will not the Judge of all the earth do right?” Gen.18:25. God has always done what is right, and it is a matter of righteousness that Christ will be publicly vindicated. The place that has been given to Him will be seen publicly in due course, but it is actually His place now. He has been put in that place of supremacy, of unassailable power, at the right hand of God: it brings a thrill to your heart to think of it. Despite what was seen publicly at the cross, and when you speak about Jesus people will know about the cross, they will have in their minds that that is the place where He hung between two common criminals; despite that, the believer is in the blessed secret of Christ’s true position, and the day of glory will display that. It will all be told out, all brought out and publicly acknowledged. The believer is in the blessed secret of it now.

In John, the Lord speaks of the place that He is going to prepare. He was going away, leaving the disciples, and they were sorrowful; but He speaks of His Father’s house, and says, “for I go to prepare you a place; and if I go and shall prepare you a place, I am coming again and shall receive you to myself, that where I am ye also may be”. The place that He took amongst men was His. No one else could take that place; it was a distinctive place, and it was His. The place that He took at the cross, no one else could take. Peter came to understand that. The Lord said to Peter, “thou canst not follow me now”, John 13:36. Peter loved the Lord, but he was not able to follow Him at that point, when He was about to face His atoning sufferings. We are not able for that place. But then the Lord speaks of His Father’s house, the place of absolute blessing, and He wants to share it with us; that is in the heart of the Lord Jesus. He speaks of the Father’s house, where all our blessings are treasured up; and He desires that that place – which He was going to prepare for them so that He could receive them there to Himself – should be shared by His own. I think He has prepared that place by going there and being there Himself.

The Lord has all His own in mind. He says, “that where I am ye also may be”. Later on, He speaks to His Father about His own: “Father, as to those whom thou hast given me, I desire that where I am they also may be with me, that they may behold my glory which thou hast given me”, John 17:24. The Lord’s desire is that His own should be with Him. We have no part in preparing that place, we could not; the work was His alone. But His desire is that His own should enter into all the fruits of that work, into the joy and the blessedness of it. It is really a promise of the Lord to His own. He also says, “I am coming again”. These promises of His should affect us. There were promises God made to Abraham, and in Hebrews it says, “All these died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them from afar off and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and sojourners on the earth” (chap.11:13). They laid hold of these promises, and they professed that as far as their part here on earth was concerned, they were strangers.

Think of the place that properly belongs to believers – we have had an impression of that. God “has raised us up together, and has made us sit down together in the heavenlies”, Eph.2:6. That conveys to me the place of privilege that God has purposed for believers: it is properly ours. If the Lord Jesus in His blessed work has removed everything obnoxious to God; if it is so that God has justified me so that no one can condemn; if He has given me of His blessed Holy Spirit, sending forth the Spirit of His own Son, then it must be so that the place He has purposed for me does indeed belong to me. Laying hold of that has an effect. It says that they “confessed that they were strangers and sojourners”; their present place was a temporary arrangement, you might say. They were travellers, strangers, here. Our place is there – together in the heavenlies. We lay hold of God’s purpose in relation to the place that Christ has prepared. The actuality awaits the coming day, but when God makes a promise, we lay hold of it, and that will have its effect with us. We live not only in faith but in the expectancy of the place that we will have, and that is properly ours. The Lord Jesus says, “I am coming again” – what a precious promise that is. The present time is the day of the Spirit, when the Spirit has come; and as we receive Him, He makes things real and living to us. There is that promise that “I am coming again and shall receive you to myself”.

The passage in Revelation 20 is very solemn: “a great white throne, and him that sat on it, from whose face the earth and the heaven fled, and place was not found for them”. That is a very solemn thing, particularly so when we consider all that is being offered in the glad tidings. It speaks of a class of people for whom a place could not be found. Everything ultimately will be consigned to its proper place; that is the reality. The Lord Jesus could say in John, “Wonder not at this, for an hour is coming in which all who are in the tombs shall hear his voice, and shall go forth; those that have practised good, to resurrection of life, and those that have done evil, to resurrection of judgment” (chap.5:28,29). This is the resurrection of the dead, when persons are raised in their sins. It says, “place was not found for them”. How solemn that is. It goes without saying: do not be found amongst such a class.
May the Lord bless the word, for His name’s sake.

articles.title: WHAT GOD HAS DONE FOR US

paragraphs.text: We spoke in the reading about what God has done for Himself, and I want to speak now about what God has done for us – in order that we might see that what God has done for us is in view of a response to Himself. We have been the objects of His favour. The hymn says:
‘But the objects of that favour
Were in chains of bondage bound;
Guilty sinners must be ransomed,
And the lost must needs be found’
(Hymn 133)

What God has done is to send His Son to seek and save that which was lost. But the lost being found has response in view. Of course, it has in view salvation from sin and eternal loss, and from banishment from the presence of God and eternity in hell. Hell is prepared for the devil and his angels; it is not prepared for man, and yet man in his will and his sins could end up there – a sober matter. But God has seen to it that there is a place for every man, woman and child in His presence, and He has provided it through the incoming of Christ and His finished work, His precious shed blood, His resurrection and His ascension. And He has given us the means whereby we might take account of that and respond to it.

That is why I have read this first section in John 3 about new birth. God has through the Spirit in effect prepared the ground in order that the seed might fall in and bear fruit a hundred-fold, for without that prepared ground there is nothing in my heart that would accept what God has done, for it says through the prophet that “The heart is deceitful above all things, and incurable”, Jer.17:9. The Authorised Version says, “desperately wicked”. The heart of man away from God has no response to God, and indeed through the prophet the nation of Israel says, “when we see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him”, Isa.53:2. But here God is acting in the power of the Holy Spirit, who is Himself God: “The wind blows where it will”; it is the action of a divine Person in sovereignty. Nicodemus says, “How can these things be?” (v.9). “How can a man be born being old? can he enter a second time into the womb of his mother and be born?”. No, that is not the answer. Sometimes the expression “born again” is used (see John 3:3 AV), and I am not despising that; but this translation says, “born anew” which is more accurate. It is not born of your mother again; it is born from an entirely new source, and that source is God; and the Spirit prepares the ground: “That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit”; God gives us a new source in the Spirit.

Now, this is not the gift of the Spirit yet; it is the action of the Spirit. “Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except any one be born anew”. I ask you to note that in verse 3 the Lord says to Nicodemus, ‘Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except any one’, and then He says again, ‘Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except any one be born of water and of Spirit’ (v.5). There is no collective salvation; there is only individual salvation – “Except any one be born of water and of Spirit”. That is to say that God has provided a way out: that is what the water speaks of. When someone is baptised – perhaps a child, in the faith of the parents in the household, you are saying effectively that this child must go out of sight, must go out of this world; the world has no claim on it, because God has a higher claim. The water is that we might have a way out; but the Spirit is that we might have a way in. God does not have in mind simply that He should take us out of the place of sin and oppression, but He has in mind to take us into a place of blessing, and the Lord speaks of it here as entering “into the kingdom of God”. The kingdom of the heavens bears somewhat on man’s responsibility; the kingdom of God is what is maintained in power by the Holy Spirit, and speaks of a place of regulation and supply. A dear brother used to remind us that you come into the kingdom to be taught and fed. God brings us out of a place, the world, where there is nothing of value in its teaching, and nothing of value in the food that it provides – husks to feed swine is all that the world can offer; and worse, it will offer you what is morally and spiritually poisonous if you will take it. But we are brought out of that and made to appreciate that there is another Man in another world.

The Spirit prepares the ground sovereignly – “thus is every one that is born of the Spirit”. And “one that is born of the Spirit” is then in a position to receive what God has done: “as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, thus must the Son of man be lifted up”. The serpent was lifted up so that they could acknowledge that what was within them had to be dealt with by another; and “if a serpent had bitten any man, and he beheld the serpent of brass, he lived”, Num.21:9. Oh, the blessing in believing: “whosoever believes on him”. It is not a question of having pre-trusted, it is a question of what we do now. So God has given us His “only-begotten Son, that whosoever believes on him may not perish, but have life eternal”. As has been said often, what God requires in His righteousness, He gives in His grace. Where are you going to get faith from? It is a gift from God. Where are you going to get repentance from? It is a gift from God. The Scripture says, “repentance towards God, and faith towards our Lord Jesus Christ”, Acts 20:21. These are gifts from God.

It has been asked, ‘Is it repentance first, or is it faith first?’. We need both: there is no point in having faith if you do not exercise it, and there is no repentance towards God without faith. God has given us both. It says, “whosoever believes on him may not perish, but have life eternal”: God has given us that. “Life eternal” in John is something that you have, and “eternal life” is something that you know. The distinction is only this – and I do not make it an arbitrary distinction – you have “eternal life” in a scene of death, you are not subject to death despite the fact that you are in a scene of death; but “life eternal” is what you know by way of relationships, what you enjoy at the present time, not only individually but collectively, of heavenly, eternal relationships; and God gives us both.

I did not read from the chapters between this one and chapter 7, but I want to touch on them briefly. The Lord speaks of the Spirit in chapter 4. The Spirit is the antidote to sin: the woman had lived a life that was not commendable; and what does the Lord say? He does not ask much of her, but He says, “this thou hast spoken truly” (v.18). He has spoken to her about the Spirit, so the Spirit is given as the antidote to sin. Then the name of the Father in chapter 5 is given as the antidote to the law. And in chapter 6, Christ as the living food is given as the antidote to the world – “Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness and died” (v.49); but “This is the bread which comes down out of heaven, that one may eat of it and not die” (v.50). God has given us what we need to make our way through this scene, surrounded by sin, and sin within; but the gift of the Spirit is there and available in order that these things might be met, and that we might be put in touch with our heavenly and eternal portion. The Spirit is that which is “springing up into eternal life”, John 4:14. And what a release “the Father” is from ‘the law’: a name of relationship and a name of grace (see John 5:16,17). Yes, a name of authority – “… be in subjection to the Father of spirits, and live” (Heb.12:9) – but a relief from the law that kept a man thirty-eight years and did nothing for him, but the Lord came in and resolved the matter in a moment.

And then that bread: “He that eats my flesh and drinks my blood”, John 6:54. Christ had to die in order that there should be living food available for us; it is bread that is out of heaven; it is suited to the place for which we are bound. It is very important to feed on the food that is suited to the place where Christ is, the place for which we are bound.

In John 8, the Lord’s words are rejected; and in the midst of that rejection, He secures the woman – “Woman, where are those thine accusers? Has no one condemned thee? And she said, No one, sir. And Jesus said to her, Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more” (vv.10,11). Then in John 9 He secures the man who was born blind, and that man’s testimony is “A man called Jesus” (v.11). And that woman and that man having been secured, He provides them with a place to go, so that in John 10 there is “one flock, one shepherd” (v.16). He takes them out of their circumstances, He does not leave them with nowhere to go. All this is God’s provision. I say this especially to my younger brethren, but I say it to all, and I say it soberly and humbly as one who wandered away from the place that God had in mind for me. I came back to it in His mercy. God has a place for you, and your place – I say without doubt – is amongst the brethren with whom He has set you, and it is your salvation to stay there. God grant that you may understand the love, the kindness, the goodness and the grace that put you in this place and would have you remain in it, true to the Lord and to His testimony in the scene of His absence.

Then in John 11, we see Christ’s power over death, and the glory of God is manifested. In John 12 we come to a place where He is loved – “There therefore they made him a supper” (v.2). We see again what Christ both has done and will do: “Now is my soul troubled, and what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour. But on account of this have I come to this hour. Father, glorify thy name. There came therefore a voice out of heaven, I both have glorified and will glorify it again” (vv.27,28). God glorified His name in Christ here, in all His walk; and then He glorified it again at the cross and in Christ’s resurrection. What a glory; and God has given us all this; He has given us the Man in whom He was glorified. Then we come to the point in John 13 that the Lord says, “Now is the Son of man glorified, and God is glorified in him. If God be glorified in him, God also shall glorify him in himself, and shall glorify him immediately” (vv.31,32). God glorifies Christ in Himself; there is an ascended Man, and God glorifies Him immediately in the heart of the assembly.

Oh, what blessings God has given us. I refer back briefly to where we read in John 7: the writer says, “the Spirit was not yet, because Jesus had not yet been glorified”. He, the Spirit, has given us a link with the Man in the glory. And the Spirit has given us power for testimony: the Lord says of those who thirst and who drink, “out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water”. The Lord says to Peter, “Unless I wash thee, thou hast not part with me” (chap.13:8). How do we have part with the Lord? I do not seek to define or limit it, but in three ways we certainly have part with Him. We have part with Him in fellowship, the fellowship of God’s Son; we have part with Him in privilege, that is to say we come together in response to His request to remember Him, and all that flows from that; and then we have part with Him in testimony. I say this soberly: for my part I believe that testimony flows from the enjoyment of fellowship and privilege. That is what I believe to be the truth, that if I give a testimony, and a person listens to it, that is not because it is my word, but because it is God’s word. Then the question arises, where would I bring that person? Where would I have them to go, and what would I have them to enjoy? Because really that is for God’s enjoyment. The fellowship of God’s Son has of course a regulating aspect, but it is for God’s enjoyment; and the privilege we have in remembering the Lord is for the enjoyment of divine Persons.

In John 14 much is opened up, but I wanted to emphasise that the Spirit is given there, as sent of the Father (vv.16,17) and then in chapter 15 the Spirit is sent of the Son (v.26). In chapter 16, the Lord says of the Spirit, “And having come” – He comes of His own volition as a divine Person (v.8). The Spirit comes here. To refer to the Spirit as a provision is insufficient to describe the blessedness of the gift of having a divine Person dwelling in us and with us for ever. What thought of man, what mere religion, gives you a man that would die for your sins, and a divine Person dwelling in you for ever? There is nothing like Christianity; there is nothing like what God has done. It is not that it is merely better; Christianity is incomparable, because Christ is incomparable. That is something to lay hold of in our souls. The world compares and assesses. God does not compare or assess: “Wherefore also God highly exalted him, and granted him a name, that which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow”, Phil.2:9,10. His purpose includes, in Ephesians 1, “to head up all things in the Christ” (v.10). God has one Man before Him, and one Man only, and God has given us faith that would accept Him.

We come to John 17: “And the glory which thou hast given me I have given them”. We touched on the matter of suitability in the earlier occasion: the glory that was given Christ is the glory of sonship, a glory that He was given in time; and He, the great administrator, has given it to us. It is made good in the gift of the Holy Spirit – “that they may be one”. It is an important matter: God is one, Father, Son and Spirit. We sometimes say that the response is equal to the revelation, and that means that the response is also one. Now, we have to hold that abstractly at the moment, but it will be so eternally; the response will be one. What is to be worked out practically amongst us is “that they may be one, as we are one”. At the present time, the thought is that the world may believe: there is a testimony to the world in the unity of the saints. A brother was in Finland on business and the hotel he was in was opposite a church; and believers were gathering – he saw them gather – and then he saw them come out again. He had no idea what they were saying to each other, nor did he know what the sign on the front of the church meant, but he could tell that they loved one another: “that they may be one, as we are one”. I just say this: could people tell that I loved my brethren? I can say that I do; but could others tell? It is “that they may be one, as we are one”. Walking in the dignity of sonship gives us high regard for one another.

Then God has given us to understand something of what the Lord went through on the way to the cross. There were those who stood by the cross (John 19:25). It is a fine perspective to have, standing by the cross of Jesus. The hymnwriter says,
‘Man the cross to Him awarded,
Man the Saviour crucified;
This world’s judgment stands recorded’
(Hymn 404)

There were those who stood by the cross and were therefore able to take account of Jesus saying, “It is finished” (v.30); and John bore witness to the blood being shed (v.35). His witness is true: God gave us a witness to the shed blood of Christ. And then He speaks to Mary, as out of death (chap.20:16,17). I add in passing, that as they entered into the tomb of Jesus, they saw the handkerchief folded up, the handkerchief that had been on His head, folded up in a distinct place by itself (v.7). That suggests Paul’s ministry: it was at that time folded up in a distinct place by itself, and God gave it to Paul to unfold, the ministry of Christ and the assembly; the glad tidings as having in mind that persons should be secured for the assembly. In Colossians it speaks about “the hope of the glad tidings” (chap.1:23); you might say, ‘the glad tidings is not about hope, it is about salvation’. It begins with that, surely: the salvation of your soul. But the glad tidings presents you with hope. It concerns “Christ Jesus our hope” (1 Tim.1:1); our hope of being with Him for ever. “Faith is the substantiating of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen”, Heb.11:1. The Christian’s hope is not a hope of doubt: people may hope for certain things and they may not come to pass, but our hope is fixed, it is in Christ: Christ Jesus is my hope. And I know that what I hope for will certainly happen.

The disciples were given that indication that there was much yet to be unfolded, then the Lord provides for the unfolding of it from Himself in glory. He also gives us a place with Himself in the presence of the Father: “I ascend to my Father and your Father, and to my God and your God”. Christ brings us into that place of nearness: when it records the words of Jacob at the end of Genesis, “Bring them, I pray thee, to me, that I may bless them” (chap.48:9), it then says of Joseph, “And he brought them nearer to him” (v.10). Joseph would know exactly how near his father wanted his sons to be. The Lord knows how near the Father wants us, He brings us nearer. When He says in John 17, “And I have made known to them thy name”, that was doubtless what He did when He was here; then He says, “and will make it known” (v.26); that is a service that continues, “will make it known”. He makes that name known to us every Lord’s day morning, in a fresh and living way, “that the love with which thou hast loved me may be in them and I in them”. He brings us near: “to my Father and your Father, and to my God and your God”. There it is, that Christ as Man can say, “my Father and your Father”; His place remains distinctive; and He can also say, “my God and your God”. He is the God
‘Well known in Jesus’ love’ (Hymn 72)

The Old Testament writer says, “no good thing will he withhold from them that walk uprightly”, Ps.84:11. God has not withheld any good things from us, beloved brethren; not one good thing is withheld.
I trust the Lord will use the word to encourage, strengthen and help us in filling out our response towards divine Persons.
May God bless it, for the Lord’s name’s sake.

I enjoyed the thought that we might respond to the desires of the Lord’s heart in asking us to remember Him in His death. I think communion in 1 Corinthians is not partaking, but association. The Lord was going away; the night in which He is betrayed He calls His loved ones around Him and says, Eat this bread and drink this cup in remembrance of Me; find it happy and strengthening to your hearts to identify yourselves with Me in My death for you here; get into company with Me, not for sorrow but for life, as ‘eating’ in John 6 indicates; the true heart finding its happiness and strength (food) in being identified on earth with Him in His last terrible service for us here. This is communion with His blood. It is to me a cup of blessing, of untold blessing. In calling Him to remembrance in His death, I place myself in company with Him there, I am engrossed with Him, and while abounding in thanksgiving because of my gain from His death, and the sense of all that He is so before me, I find and feel that no other place in this scene so suits my heart as that which sets me in identification and association with Him at the moment when He is pre-eminently before me.

I enjoyed the meeting or rather the place of meeting, feeling how near we were to the Lord, how enough He is for our hearts, how His presence refuses everything that is unfit for Him, and yet how perfectly happy, lacking nothing, we are there.

I said my desire for each one was that in His presence we might have deeper memories of His death. I feel that as we are to go out of this world in Christ’s death, we ought to be identifying ourselves with it here. I spoke on enjoying His presence individually and collectively – the greatness of it. We should seek it, for by His presence alone can our information be moulded and effective, otherwise the truth has little power, it is like so much ore without a model for it.
Extract from JB Stoney New Series Vol.8 pp.145,146

No one will ever understand speaking to God in the assembly until he understands speaking to God in his closet. I believe the closet is less understood than the holiest, at least mentally. The first thing is the closet, that is to say, the door shut to all others save God and yourself; you speak to God in secret. No doubt Moses had been accustomed to do that; he could never have become the man he was in the service of God had he not been accustomed to speak to God in secret. His brother Aaron too could never have had the place he had as priest in Israel save that he had been accustomed to speak to God in secret. God says, “I know him,” one of the finest things that could be said of any of us by God. If any man love God the same is known of God, and we become known to God as we, as it were, knock at His door. As we seek access, He opens it; the door is opened, as I have been saying, and as you enter your closet and shut your door and turn to God in the light in which He has drawn near to you in your circumstances; you will soon find the holiest, and you will soon find that your closet has become the holiest. The holiest is the presence of God, but in Jesus; it is what Jesus is before God. It is as if God would say to you, ‘These are the things that engage Me, and Christ is the centre’ and you take a place there. You are not the centre; the more you draw near, the more you see that Christ is the centre and all around is holy. Like the holy vessels of the sanctuary, all were anointed and all were in perfect keeping within; they stood in relation to the ark. So that it was no new thing for Moses to speak to God; he was accustomed to do it. Nor can any serve God or be honoured of God save one who speaks to Him, who makes everything a matter of speaking to God.
Extract from JT New Series Vol.99 p.150
